Elara’s workshop smelled of brass filings and old dust, a scent that had permeated her clothes for forty years. She was a master of precision, a woman who believed that time was a river flowing strictly forward, carrying all things toward their inevitable end. But on this particular Tuesday, as rain lashed against the high windows, she felt a strange dissonance in the ticking of the shop’s grandfather clocks. It wasn’t just a sound; it was a weight.

She had been working on a commission for the Mayor, a piece meant to mark the city’s bicentennial. But her hands, guided by an intuition she couldn’t name, had altered the escapement mechanism. Instead of the standard anchor, she had crafted a reverse-gear assembly, delicate as a spider’s web, designed to pull the pendulum back rather than push it forward.

When she finally wound the mainspring, the clock did not tick. It *hissed*. A low, resonant hum filled the room, vibrating in her teeth. The second hand, a slender needle of polished steel, began to move counter-clockwise.

Elara held her breath. The dust motes dancing in the shaft of light from the window stopped their chaotic swirl. Slow
